extracted.intended_audience: European patent attorneys, EPO practitioners, patent applicants, IP lawyers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and case-law-centred evaluation of when and how the description of a European patent application must be amended to align with allowable claims under Article 84 EPC and the EPO Guidelines; practical and procedural consequences are discussed. Useful for prosecuting/defending European patents and advising clients on amendment strategy and appeal risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must not contradict allowable claims (Guidelines H-V 2.7; F-IV 4.3(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guidelines for Examination require substantial amendments such that the description does not contradict the allowable claims (H-V, 2.7 and F-IV, 4.3(iii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants are expected to align the description with the scope of allowable claims; the Guidance is an EPO-specific practice and may require deletion or clarification of description passages that conflict with the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delete or disclaim subject-matter not covered by the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants are required either to delete subject matter no longer covered by the claims or explicitly state that the offending subject matter does not fall under the scope of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical considerations: applicants are often reluctant to remove or disclaim description material because amendments can affect claim interpretation (e.g., doctrine of equivalents), and because of the time and cost involved in extensive description edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims shall be clear, concise and supported by the description (Article 84 EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought. They shall be clear and concise and be supported by the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory basis cited by the Board in T 1024/18 for requiring descriptions to be consistent with claims. The support requirement is treated as a separate limb (support distinct from clarity and conciseness).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Supported by the description' requires support by the whole description (T 1024/18)
rubrics_metrics.description: "'supported by the description' is a distinct requirement to clarity and means 'supported by the whole description'" (Board reasoning in T 1024/18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: According to T 1024/18, it is not sufficient that a single passage supports the claims if other portions of the description give a different or contradictory meaning; the entire description must be consistent with the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims should be clear from their wording alone (Guidelines F-IV 4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Each claim must be read giving the words the meaning and scope which they normally have in the relevant art" and the Guidelines "require the claim to be amended whereby the meaning is clear from the wording of the claim alone" (F-IV, 4.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This guideline supports the idea that claims need not rely on the description for clarity. There is a tension between this principle and the view that the whole description must support the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate (contrary) interpretation: support limited to basis for claimed subject-matter (T 1989/18)
rubrics_metrics.description: T 1989/18 held that Art. 84 EPC requires the claims to be supported by the description only to the extent that the claims should not include subject matter that does not have basis in the description; additional subject matter in the description that does not appear in the claims is not prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This represents a less onerous approach — inconsistencies in the description that do not undermine the claims' clarity/support (in the sense of added matter) need not be removed. The Board in T 1024/18 expressly disagreed with this view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disparity between description and claims can make claim scope unclear (Article 69 EPC / interpretative role of description)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an argument that the description should be used to interpret the claims (Article 69 EPC), and thus that a disparity between the description and the claims may make the scope of the claims unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports the rationale for requiring alignment: if the description conflicts with claims, readers (or courts) might be uncertain about claim scope. However, EPO Guidelines elsewhere emphasize claim wording as primary for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural consequence: failure to file amended description with allowable amended claims on appeal risks revocation
rubrics_metrics.description: In T 1024/18 the patentee failed to file an amended description in line with the auxiliary request (AR) claims, and the Board of Appeal therefore revoked the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should note that not providing an amended description that aligns with allowable claims (including on appeal) can lead to revocation for procedural efficiency and without remittal to the opposition division.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO Guidelines are idiosyncratic compared to other jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: No other jurisdiction (as far as the author is aware) forces applicants to amend the description in line with the allowed claims; this requirement is an idiosyncrasy of European patent practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advising international clients, consider jurisdictional differences and the additional burden/time/cost the EPO's approach may impose versus other offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative weight of Board decisions and distribution status matters in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: T 1024/18 has been given a 'C' distribution and appears in 'Selected Decisions', whereas T 1989/18 had a 'D' distribution and did not appear as a Selected Decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should consider the distribution/status of Board decisions (e.g., Selected Decision, distribution letter) as an indicator of how persuasive or likely-to-be-followed a ruling may be in practice, although disagreements between Boards remain possible and may eventually require an EBA referral.
